terminal.description: A shell in your workspace where the demo signs two customers in and prints the log lines.

tasks.title: Catch a secret in the log
tasks.description:
Before you change anything, prove the hole. In `src/reproduce.js`, implement `reproduceLeak()`.

Sign in once through the original `signIn()` with a fresh `openDb()`, using a customer from `seed.js`, and collect every log line in an array. Return an object with:

- `form`: the `{ email, password }` you signed in with
- `log`: every line `signIn()` logged, in order
- `result`: exactly what `signIn()` returned

The check runs your function against the original `signIn.js`. It passes when `log` and `result` are real and a password, a session token or a password hash shows in a log line or in the message.
nextSteps: Run `node src/demo.js` and read every log line it prints.
Write a log function that pushes each line into an array.
Sign in once with it and keep the result.
Run the demo again and find the secret in what you return.
hints: signIn takes the log as a function, so you decide where its lines go.
const log = [] and (line) => log.push(line) collect every line signIn writes.
Sign in as cosmo@example.com with the wrong password tin-lantern-5, and return the form, the lines and the result.

tasks.title: Keep secrets out of the log and the page
tasks.description:
Fix `signIn(db, log, form)` in `src/signIn.js` so no secret ever leaves it, except the token handed back to the customer who signed in.

- The right password still signs in and returns `{ ok: true, token }`, with the token saved as a session.
- A wrong password, or an email nobody has, returns `{ ok: false, message }`, with the same message for both.
- No log line holds a password, a session token or a password hash, and no message holds a password or a hash.
- Nothing secret is printed to the console.
- Every attempt still logs a line with its email.

The check signs in with right and wrong passwords and an unknown email, and looks for every secret in each log line, each message and the console.
nextSteps: Find every place one of them leaves the function.
Write each log line from what happened, not from what was typed.
Run `node src/demo.js` and read the log lines again.
hints: Three secrets pass through: the password typed, the stored hash and the new session token. Only the token should ever leave, and only in the result.
Logging the whole form logs the password with it. A log line can name the email and the outcome without copying the form.
Log a line such as `sign in failed for ${form.email}` or `signed in ${form.email}`, and make the wrong password message the same plain sentence as for an unknown email.

videos.title: Why a site keeps a hash, not the password

tasks.title: Write the test that would have caught it
tasks.description:
Write vitest tests in `src/signIn.test.js` that guard this hole for good. Use a fresh `openDb()` and a log that collects its lines in an array.

The check runs your test file three times: beside the original `signIn.js` (it must fail), beside a correct fix (it must pass) and beside a fix that keeps the session token out of the log but still logs the form (it must fail).
nextSteps: Sign in with the right password and check no line holds the token.
Add a check the token-only fix gets wrong.
hints: expect(line).not.toContain(secret) says a secret is not in a line. Loop over every line.
The token-only fix still logs the whole form. What is in the form?
For every line, also expect it not to contain the password you signed in with, for a right and for a wrong password.
